questions.title: The OSI Model's Seven Layers
questions.prompt: What are the seven layers of the OSI model, and why do most network troubleshooting methodologies start at Layer 1 and work upward instead of starting at the application layer?
questions.modelAnswer: The seven OSI layers, bottom to top, are Physical (cabling, signals), Data Link (MAC addressing, switching), Network (IP addressing, routing), Transport (TCP/UDP, port numbers), Session (managing a connection's session state), Presentation (data formatting/encoding), and Application (the actual protocol the user-facing program speaks, like HTTP). The common mnemonic is 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.' Troubleshooting works bottom-up because each layer depends entirely on the ones below it functioning correctly -- a problem that looks like an application-layer issue (a website won't load) can't actually be diagnosed as an application problem until physical connectivity, addressing, and routing below it are confirmed working, since a broken lower layer will produce the exact same symptom as a broken upper layer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with a 'this website won't load' complaint. Before I ever look at the application itself, I check the cable and link light -- Layer 1 -- because no amount of debugging the app matters if the physical connection is down. Then I think about which devices operate at which layer: switches work at Layer 2 using MAC addresses, routers work at Layer 3 using IP addresses, so if I suspect the problem is routing-related I know exactly which device to go check. Working bottom-up isn't just a memorized rule for me -- it's genuinely the fastest path to a root cause, because ruling out the cheap, simple layers first saves me from chasing an application bug that was never actually there.
commonMistakes: Confusing which layer switches (Layer 2, MAC addresses) versus routers (Layer 3, IP addresses) operate at
Starting troubleshooting at the application layer and wasting time before checking basic connectivity
Forgetting the Session and Presentation layers exist and lumping their functions into Application
Treating the OSI model as purely academic trivia instead of a practical troubleshooting order
keyPoints: Seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Mnemonic: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away
Bottom-up troubleshooting rules out simple causes before chasing complex ones
Switches operate at Layer 2 (MAC); routers operate at Layer 3 (IP)

questions.title: The CIA Triad
questions.prompt: Explain the three legs of the CIA triad -- confidentiality, integrity, and availability -- and give a real-world breach example that illustrates each one being violated.
questions.modelAnswer: Confidentiality means only authorized people or systems can see the data -- violated when the 2017 Equifax breach exposed 147 million people's personal records to attackers who had no business seeing them. Integrity means the data can be trusted not to have been altered without authorization -- violated when someone tampers with accounting records, where the real damage isn't that the data was seen, it's that it can no longer be trusted. Availability means authorized users can actually get to the data or system when they need it -- violated by a DDoS attack that floods a service until legitimate users can't reach it at all. Controls map differently to each leg: encryption and access control protect confidentiality, hashing and digital signatures protect integrity, and redundancy, backups, and DDoS protection protect availability.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always find it clearer to anchor each leg to a real incident rather than just defining the words. Equifax is the clean confidentiality example -- 147 million records exposed, nothing altered, just seen by people who shouldn't have seen it. For integrity, I think about an insider quietly editing financial records -- nobody's blocked from anything, but now you can't trust the numbers, which is often worse than a confidentiality breach because it can go unnoticed for a long time. For availability, a DDoS attack is the textbook case -- nothing is stolen or changed, the service is just unreachable. The reason I care about naming which leg is actually in play is that it changes my response: a confidentiality incident means figuring out what was exposed and to whom, an integrity incident means figuring out what's actually still trustworthy, and an availability incident means getting the service back up, and those are very different first moves.
commonMistakes: Treating CIA as a checklist instead of three competing priorities that a response has to weigh differently
Assuming every incident violates all three legs equally
Forgetting integrity failures can be silent -- nobody notices until long after the damage is done
Confusing availability with uptime SLAs only, rather than a security property that can be deliberately attacked
keyPoints: Confidentiality = only authorized parties can see it
Integrity = the data can be trusted not to have been altered
Availability = authorized users can reach it when they need it
A given incident usually centers on one leg, which should drive the response
Controls map differently per leg: encryption/access control, hashing/signatures, redundancy/backups

questions.title: TCP's Three-Way Handshake vs. UDP
questions.prompt: Walk through TCP's three-way handshake step by step, and explain why some protocols (like DNS and VoIP) use UDP instead of TCP despite UDP offering no delivery guarantees.
questions.modelAnswer: The handshake is SYN (client proposes a connection with an initial sequence number), SYN-ACK (server acknowledges and proposes its own sequence number), and ACK (client acknowledges the server's number) -- after those three packets, both sides have a reliable, ordered connection and can start exchanging data. TCP guarantees that data arrives, arrives in order, and gets retransmitted if lost, which costs overhead: the handshake itself, plus ongoing acknowledgments. UDP skips all of that -- no handshake, no guarantee, just send and hope. DNS mostly uses UDP because a single quick request/response doesn't justify handshake overhead, though it falls back to TCP for larger responses like zone transfers. VoIP and streaming use UDP because a late packet is a useless packet -- by the time TCP would retransmit a dropped audio packet, that moment in the call has already passed, so they'd rather drop it and move on than wait.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw the three packets out -- SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK -- and point out that the sequence numbers exchanged there are what let TCP reassemble data in the right order and know what's missing if something gets lost. Then I'd explain the UDP choice as a deliberate tradeoff, not a weakness: DNS doesn't want to pay handshake overhead for a single lookup, and VoIP specifically doesn't want retransmission at all, because a retransmitted audio packet for something said two seconds ago is worthless -- the call has already moved on. So the protocol choice always comes down to whether a late, resent packet is still useful or not.
commonMistakes: Thinking UDP is 'insecure' rather than simply unreliable by design
Forgetting DNS can fall back to TCP for larger responses like zone transfers
Assuming the handshake happens for every packet rather than once per connection
Confusing sequence numbers' purpose (ordering/reassembly) with encryption, which TCP doesn't provide at all
keyPoints: Handshake steps: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK with exchanged sequence numbers
TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery via retransmission
UDP is connectionless and low-overhead, with no delivery guarantee
Protocol choice depends on whether a late/resent packet is still useful (DNS/VoIP say no)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes all three handshake steps

questions.title: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Encryption, and How TLS Uses Both
questions.prompt: What's the difference between symmetric encryption (like AES) and asymmetric encryption (like RSA), and why does TLS use both instead of just one or the other?
questions.modelAnswer: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting -- it's fast, but both sides need the same key, which creates a key-distribution problem: how do you safely hand that key to someone over a network an attacker might be watching? Asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair -- anyone can encrypt with the public key, but only the matching private key can decrypt -- which solves the distribution problem since the public key doesn't need to be kept secret, but it's computationally much slower. TLS uses both for exactly this reason: it uses asymmetric encryption during the handshake to securely agree on a one-time symmetric session key, then switches to fast symmetric encryption (like AES) for the actual data transfer, getting asymmetric's safe key exchange and symmetric's speed in the same connection.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as solving two different problems, not competing for the same job. Symmetric is fast but has the 'how do I hand you the key safely' problem. Asymmetric solves exactly that problem because the public key can be shared openly, but it's too slow to encrypt an entire web session with. TLS's answer is to use asymmetric crypto just once, at the start, to agree on a symmetric session key, and then hand off to AES for everything after that. So when someone asks why TLS doesn't 'just pick one,' my answer is that it's not picking the better one -- it's using each one for the part of the problem it's actually good at.
commonMistakes: Assuming asymmetric encryption is simply 'more secure' rather than solving a different problem (key distribution)
Thinking a private key is ever transmitted to the other party
Believing TLS uses asymmetric encryption for the entire session rather than just the handshake
Mixing up which key encrypts and which key decrypts in an asymmetric exchange
keyPoints: Symmetric = one shared key, fast, but has a key-distribution problem
Asymmetric = public/private key pair, solves distribution but is computationally slow
TLS uses asymmetric crypto only during the handshake to agree on a session key
TLS then switches to fast symmetric encryption (AES) for the actual connection

questions.title: Why SMS Codes Aren't Strong MFA
questions.prompt: What are the three categories of authentication factors, and why does NIST flag SMS-based one-time codes as a weaker MFA option compared to an authenticator app or a hardware security key?
questions.modelAnswer: The three factor categories are something you know (a password), something you have (a phone, a hardware key), and something you are (a fingerprint). Real MFA requires factors from at least two different categories -- a password plus a security question is still just two 'know' factors and isn't real MFA. NIST SP 800-63B flags SMS-based codes as a restricted option because they're vulnerable to SIM swapping (an attacker convinces a carrier to move your number to their SIM) and SS7 interception (exploiting flaws in the telecom signaling protocol), both of which bypass the code without ever touching your device. A TOTP authenticator app generates its 30-second rotating codes locally on the device with no telecom dependency at all, and hardware keys built on FIDO2/WebAuthn are phishing-resistant because they cryptographically bind the authentication to the actual origin domain -- a fake look-alike login page simply can't complete the exchange, since the key checks the domain itself, not just what's displayed on screen.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clear up is that two 'know' factors don't count as MFA just because you typed two different things. Then for SMS specifically, I'd point to SIM swapping as the concrete attack -- the attacker doesn't need to touch your phone at all, just convince your carrier to move your number, and now your 'something you have' factor is sitting in their hands instead of yours. A TOTP app avoids that because it's generating codes locally with no carrier involved. Hardware keys go a step further and are genuinely phishing-resistant, because the key itself checks that it's talking to the real domain before it'll respond -- so even if someone's fooled by a perfect-looking fake login page, the key just won't cooperate with it.
commonMistakes: Counting two 'something you know' factors as real multi-factor authentication
Assuming SMS-based MFA is just as strong as any other MFA method
Not knowing specifically why hardware keys are phishing-resistant (origin binding, not just being a physical device)
Confusing TOTP app security with SMS security because both display a six-digit code
keyPoints: Three factor categories: something you know, have, are
Real MFA needs factors from at least two different categories
SMS codes are vulnerable to SIM swapping and SS7 interception
TOTP apps generate codes locally with no telecom dependency
FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys are phishing-resistant via origin binding

questions.title: SOC Analyst Tiers: 1, 2, and 3
questions.prompt: Describe what a Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 SOC analyst each actually do day to day, using a real alert type (like a 'multiple failed logins followed by one success' alert) to show how each tier would handle it differently.
questions.modelAnswer: Tier 1 triages the live alert queue, applies playbooks, and escalates whatever's beyond their authority or tools. Tier 2 does deeper investigation and containment on whatever Tier 1 escalates. Tier 3 doesn't primarily work the queue at all -- they do proactive threat hunting and tune the detection rules themselves. For a 'five failed logins then one success' alert: Tier 1 checks whether the login location/device is plausible and decides whether to escalate; Tier 2, once it's escalated, pulls related logs, checks for any signs of lateral movement, and makes the containment call; Tier 3 would instead ask why the rule only fired on the fifth failure and not earlier, and whether a tighter threshold or a related pattern should become a permanent new detection. The realistic career path from Tier 1 to Tier 2 is roughly one to two years.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the tiers by what each one is actually accountable for, not just seniority. Tier 1 is the first set of eyes and the triage judgment call -- does this look real, does it need to go up. Tier 2 picks up anything escalated and does the real digging -- what else did this account touch, do we need to isolate something. Tier 3 is a different kind of work entirely -- they're not reacting to the queue, they're asking 'why didn't our rules catch this earlier' and building the detection that would. On that same failed-login alert, I'd expect Tier 3's real contribution to be a new or tightened correlation rule, not working that specific ticket at all.
commonMistakes: Thinking Tier 3 just handles 'the hardest tickets' rather than doing genuinely proactive, non-queue-driven work
Assuming every alert has to escalate all the way to Tier 3 eventually
Underestimating how much real judgment Tier 1 triage requires, not just checklist-following
Treating the tiers as purely a seniority ladder instead of a difference in scope of authority and depth
keyPoints: Tier 1 = triage, playbooks, escalation
Tier 2 = deeper investigation and containment on escalated items
Tier 3 = proactive threat hunting and detection-rule tuning, not queue work
Tiers differ in scope of authority and depth, not just seniority
Realistic Tier 1 to Tier 2 progression is about one to two years

questions.title: What a SIEM Actually Does
questions.prompt: A SIEM is often described as 'just a place logs get stored.' What are the four core functions a real SIEM performs, and why is correlation -- not storage -- the part that actually makes it valuable?
questions.modelAnswer: A SIEM's four core functions are centralization (pulling logs from many sources into one place), normalization-driven correlation (connecting related events across sources), alerting (surfacing the connections that matter), and retention (keeping the history around for investigation and compliance). The value isn't the storage itself -- a log management tool can store everything forever and never notice anything. The value is correlation: a firewall logs a port scan from a given IP, and minutes later antivirus on a completely different device logs an alert, also tied to that same source IP. Neither entry alone looks urgent. It's only by correlating them across two unrelated log sources, by a shared field like source IP, that two mundane-looking entries become one meaningful alert worth a human's attention.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on 'just storage,' because that's actually describing a log management tool, not a SIEM. What makes a SIEM worth the name is that it's actively looking for connections between events that, on their own, nobody would flag -- a port scan here, an antivirus hit there, minutes apart, on different machines, tied together only by a shared IP. That correlation is the entire point. Raw storage with no correlation logic is just an expensive filing cabinet.
commonMistakes: Conflating a SIEM with plain log storage or log management
Assuming more retention automatically means better detection
Forgetting alerting still requires a human triage step afterward
Not realizing correlation depends on normalized fields across differently-formatted log sources first
keyPoints: Four core functions: centralize, correlate, alert, retain
Correlation -- not storage -- is the real differentiator
Correlation requires normalized fields that mean the same thing across sources
A SIEM's alerts still require a human triage step on top

questions.title: KQL vs. SQL
questions.prompt: You're comfortable with SQL. What is KQL (Kusto Query Language), where is it used in a Microsoft security stack, and what are the real syntactic differences you'd need to adjust to coming from a SQL background?
questions.modelAnswer: KQL powers Microsoft Sentinel, Defender XDR's advanced hunting, and Azure Data Explorer. It's pipe-based (using |) and imperative -- each stage transforms the output of the stage before it, in the exact order you wrote it, top to bottom. SQL is declarative, where SELECT/FROM/WHERE's written order doesn't dictate execution order. A query like `SigninLogs | where ResultType != "0" | project UserPrincipalName, ResultType` reads literally as 'start from this table, then filter, then pick these columns' -- the same underlying logic as a SQL WHERE plus SELECT, but with the execution order made explicit in the syntax itself. KQL is also case-sensitive by default, which most SQL dialects are not.
questions.professionalAnswer: My honest first instinct coming from SQL was to assume KQL is 'basically SQL with different keywords,' and that assumption gets you in trouble fast. The pipe syntax means I have to think about my query as a literal pipeline, reading top to bottom in the order things actually happen, rather than SQL's declarative style where I can write WHERE before SELECT and it doesn't matter. And the case sensitivity catches people off guard constantly -- a column name or string comparison that would just work in most SQL dialects can silently fail to match in KQL if the casing's off.
commonMistakes: Assuming KQL is just SQL with renamed keywords and getting tripped up by case sensitivity
Writing KQL as if clause order didn't matter, the way it doesn't in declarative SQL
Not recognizing the same analytical question needs to be re-ordered conceptually, even though the result is equivalent
Forgetting KQL is used beyond Sentinel, including Defender XDR advanced hunting and Azure Data Explorer
keyPoints: KQL powers Sentinel, Defender XDR advanced hunting, and Azure Data Explorer
KQL is pipe-based and imperative -- execution order matches the order written
SQL is declarative -- clause order in the text doesn't dictate execution order
KQL is case-sensitive by default

questions.title: The Four Phases of the NIST Incident Response Lifecycle
questions.prompt: What are the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, and why is it usually drawn as a cycle rather than a straight line?
questions.modelAnswer: The four phases are Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity. It's drawn as a cycle because Post-Incident Activity -- the lessons-learned step -- feeds directly back into Preparation: the plan, tooling, and detections that determine whether the next incident is caught quickly or missed entirely are shaped by what was learned from the last one. Walking a compromised workstation through all four: Preparation is having a plan and the right access ready before anything happens; Detection & Analysis is confirming the alert is real; Containment/Eradication/Recovery is isolating it, removing the actual cause, and bringing it back clean; Post-Incident Activity is writing up what worked and feeding any new detection idea back into the SIEM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd emphasize that this isn't a one-time checklist you run through once -- it's explicitly a loop, and NIST draws it that way on purpose. Every incident's Post-Incident Activity step should change something about Preparation for next time, whether that's a new playbook step, a tooling gap that got exposed, or a detection rule that should have existed. If a team treats Post-Incident Activity as 'write the report and move on' without that feedback loop actually closing, they're skipping the one phase that makes the next incident go better than this one did.
commonMistakes: Treating the lifecycle as a one-time linear checklist instead of a continuous loop
Skipping Post-Incident Activity once systems are back online
Conflating Containment, Eradication, and Recovery into one undifferentiated step
Treating Preparation as a one-time setup rather than something revisited after every incident

questions.title: Zero Trust, Conceptually: Why the Perimeter Model Stopped Working
questions.prompt: At a conceptual level, what does 'zero trust' actually mean, and what changed in how companies operate that made the old 'castle and moat' perimeter model stop being a safe assumption?
questions.modelAnswer: The old perimeter model assumed an enterprise-owned network, company-managed devices, trust granted once at login, and resources that all lived inside the perimeter. Zero trust, grounded in NIST SP 800-207, instead assumes no implicit trust at all -- every request is verified explicitly, regardless of where it originates or what trusted it before. Four real shifts broke the old assumption: cloud and SaaS adoption (resources no longer live inside any single perimeter), remote and hybrid work, BYOD and third-party access, and the plain fact that an attacker who gets past the perimeter once has historically been able to move laterally with little resistance once inside. Zero trust isn't a single product you buy -- it's a set of architectural principles applied continuously to every request.
questions.professionalAnswer: I like the castle-and-moat analogy because it makes the flaw obvious: once you're inside the castle gate, you can walk into any room. The old model trusted you fully the moment you got past the one checkpoint. Zero trust is more like checking a badge at every single door, not just the front gate -- because cloud apps, remote workers, and personal devices mean there effectively isn't one front gate anymore, and because once an attacker is in, you don't want them to have the run of the place just because they got past the first checkpoint.
commonMistakes: Thinking zero trust means 'trust nothing, allow nothing' rather than explicit continuous verification
Assuming it's a single product to buy rather than an architecture applied everywhere
Believing it only applies to remote users, not to resources inside a traditional office network too
Conflating zero trust with simply replacing a VPN
keyPoints: Zero trust = no implicit trust, explicit per-request verification (NIST SP 800-207)
Old model assumed an owned network, managed devices, and one-time login trust
Broken by cloud/SaaS adoption, remote work, BYOD, and unchecked lateral movement
Zero trust is an architecture applied continuously, not a product

questions.title: Subnetting a /26 Network
questions.prompt: Given the network 192.168.1.0/26, what is the subnet mask, how many usable host addresses does it provide, and what are the network and broadcast addresses?
questions.modelAnswer: A /26 mask is 255.255.255.192 -- 26 network bits leave 6 host bits, and 2^6 is 64 total addresses in the block. Subtract the network address and the broadcast address (every block reserves exactly one of each) and you get 62 usable host addresses. For 192.168.1.0/26, the network address is 192.168.1.0 and the broadcast address is 192.168.1.63, making the usable range 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.62. Beyond the math, smaller subnets are also a deliberate security tool: splitting a network into tighter blocks limits the size of each broadcast domain and the blast radius if any one segment is compromised.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fast way I check this in my head is the block-size trick: 256 minus the mask's last octet value (192) gives 64, so the block starts at a multiple of 64 -- here, 192.168.1.0 -- and runs up to the next multiple minus one, which is .63. That's your broadcast address, and the two endpoints of that range are reserved, so .1 through .62 are what's actually usable. I'd also point out that the reason I'd choose a /26 instead of leaving everything on one big /24 isn't just address planning -- it's that a smaller subnet keeps the broadcast domain tighter and limits how far a problem on one segment can spread.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract the network and broadcast addresses from the total block size
Miscounting host bits and confusing a /26 with a /25 or /27
Assuming the broadcast address is always .255 rather than the last address in that specific block
Not connecting subnet size choice to a security/segmentation rationale
keyPoints: 64 total addresses in the block, 62 usable
Network address = 192.168.1.0, broadcast address = 192.168.1.63

questions.title: Spotting a Port Scan in Wireshark
questions.prompt: You're looking at a Wireshark capture and see an unusually large number of SYN packets going out to many different destination ports on the same host, with very few SYN-ACK replies. What does this traffic pattern indicate, and what display filter would you use to isolate it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the signature of a port scan: a normal connection completes exactly one three-packet handshake on one port, while a scanner sends bare SYNs across many ports and only gets SYN-ACKs back from the ports that happen to be open -- closed ports typically reply with a RST instead of silence, and filtered ports may not reply at all, which is why the SYN-ACK count looks so lopsided against the SYN count. To isolate it in Wireshark, filters like `tcp.flags.syn==1 and tcp.flags.ack==0` narrow the view to bare SYNs, and combining that with `ip.addr==<suspect-ip>` scopes it to the specific host generating the pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway for me is the ratio, not just the volume -- lots of SYNs, almost no completed handshakes, spread across many destination ports instead of one. A real connection always finishes its three packets on a single port; a scan is fundamentally many incomplete attempts. I'd filter with `tcp.flags.syn==1 and tcp.flags.ack==0` to pull out just the bare SYNs, then add `ip.addr==` for the source I'm suspicious of, and I'd also expect to see some RSTs coming back from the closed ports rather than total silence on every one.
commonMistakes: Mistaking a port scan for a volume-based DoS/flood, which is a different kind of attack with a different intent
Not knowing the normal baseline (exactly one completed handshake per real connection) to compare against
Forgetting closed ports often reply with RST rather than staying silent
Filtering on `ip.addr` alone without also narrowing to the relevant TCP flags, pulling in unrelated traffic
keyPoints: Many SYNs with few SYN-ACKs across many ports from one source = port scan signature
A normal connection completes exactly one three-packet handshake on one port
Useful filters: `tcp.flags.syn==1 and tcp.flags.ack==0`, `ip.addr==`, `tcp.port==`
Closed ports often reply RST, not silence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the port-scan pattern

questions.title: Building an Isolated Home Lab for Security Practice
questions.prompt: You want to build a home lab to practice attacking and defending systems safely -- a Kali Linux attacker VM, a Metasploitable2 vulnerable target, and a pfSense virtual firewall. What's the single most important network configuration decision in that lab, and what goes wrong if you get it wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: The single most important decision is the hypervisor's network mode for the lab VMs -- they need to run on Host-Only or Internal Network, never Bridged. Bridged mode puts the lab VMs directly onto the real local network, which means Metasploitable2's deliberately vulnerable services, or live exploit traffic coming from Kali, could actually reach other real devices on the home or work network, or the internet. That turns a practice lab into real unauthorized access against systems that were never in scope, which carries real legal exposure under laws like the CFAA even if it was unintentional.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat this as the one setting I check before anything else, because it's the easiest thing to get wrong and the most consequential. Bridged networking is often the default in a hypervisor's new-VM wizard, which is exactly why it's dangerous -- it's easy to click past it without thinking. I always confirm Host-Only or Internal Network is set before I ever power on Metasploitable2, specifically because that VM is full of intentional vulnerabilities, and I don't want any of that reachable by anything outside the lab, on purpose or by accident.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to Bridged mode because it's often the easiest or default option in the hypervisor
Assuming a firewall VM like pfSense alone provides sufficient isolation without also checking the hypervisor's network mode
Not treating Metasploitable2's deliberate vulnerabilities as a reason to be extra careful about exposure
Treating 'it's just a lab' as meaning legal authorization and scope don't matter
keyPoints: Use Host-Only or Internal Network isolation, never Bridged
Kali = attacker VM, Metasploitable2 = deliberately vulnerable target, pfSense = virtual firewall
Getting the network mode wrong can expose real devices/networks to lab traffic
Legal and authorization awareness applies even in a personal lab

questions.title: Granting Limited sudo Access With the Sudoers File
questions.prompt: Write a sudoers entry that lets the user jsmith run only `systemctl restart nginx` as root, without a password prompt. Why must this be edited with visudo instead of a normal text editor, and why does the command need to be an absolute path?
questions.code:
-- Goal: let user jsmith restart the nginx service as root,
-- without giving jsmith full root access or a password prompt.
questions.modelAnswer: The sudoers syntax is `who where=(as whom) what`. The entry would be `jsmith ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx`. It must be edited with `visudo` instead of a normal editor because visudo validates the file's syntax before saving -- editing /etc/sudoers directly with a typo can silently break sudo entirely, and visudo refuses to save an invalid file, protecting against locking yourself out of sudo altogether. The command must be an absolute path because a relative or bare command name would be resolved against jsmith's own PATH, which jsmith could manipulate to point `systemctl` at a malicious script -- turning a narrowly scoped 'restart nginx only' grant into effectively unrestricted root code execution.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write exactly the line that grants only this one command, not `ALL` commands, because the whole point of the request was limiting what jsmith can do as root. I always use visudo for the edit -- it's not optional for me, because a broken sudoers file from a typo in a direct edit can lock out sudo access for everyone, and visudo catches that before it's saved. The absolute path matters more than it looks like it should: if I just wrote `systemctl` without the full path, jsmith could put their own script named `systemctl` earlier in their PATH and I'd have handed them root execution of whatever they wanted, not just a service restart.
questions.example:
jsmith ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx

# Always validate and save with:
sudo visudo
commonMistakes: Editing /etc/sudoers directly instead of with visudo
Granting ALL commands instead of scoping to the one command actually needed
Forgetting the absolute-path requirement, opening a PATH-hijacking hole
Adding NOPASSWD without a deliberate reason, or omitting it when password-free automation was actually the goal
keyPoints: Sudoers syntax: who where=(as whom) what
visudo validates syntax before saving, preventing a lockout
Absolute paths prevent PATH-hijacking
NOPASSWD should be a deliberate choice, not a default
/etc/sudoers.d/ allows modular, per-user grants

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct sudoers syntax for the specific grant
Correctly explains why visudo is required
Correctly explains the absolute-path requirement

questions.title: Reading Key Windows Security Event IDs
questions.prompt: You see this sequence in a Windows Security event log for one user account within a short window: Event ID 4720, then 4728, then 4672. What does each event ID mean individually, and why is this specific sequence a red flag?
questions.modelAnswer: 4720 means an account was created, 4728 means it was added to a security-enabled global group, and 4672 means special admin privileges were assigned at logon. Any one of these alone could be routine IT provisioning. But this exact sequence, in a short window -- create a brand-new account, immediately add it to a privileged group, and have that account immediately log on with admin rights -- is a textbook attacker-provisioning pattern for a persistent backdoor account, which doesn't typically match how normal onboarding plays out (a new hire's account usually isn't created and granted admin privileges and logged into within minutes). The other two core logon IDs worth knowing alongside these are 4624 (successful logon) and 4625 (failed logon, a brute-force signal).
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't look at any single one of these IDs in isolation -- that's the trap. 4720 by itself is just account provisioning, which happens all the time. It's the combination and the timing that makes me suspicious: an account that didn't exist an hour ago is now sitting in a privileged group and has already logged on with admin rights. My next step would be checking who actually performed the 4720 and 4728 actions and whether there's a change ticket that matches, because that's the difference between routine provisioning and someone standing up their own backdoor.
commonMistakes: Evaluating each event ID in isolation instead of recognizing the combined sequence as the real signal
Not knowing 4672 specifically flags admin-level privilege assignment, not just any logon
Confusing 4720 (account created) with similarly-numbered IDs like 4722 (account enabled)
Dismissing the pattern as routine IT work without checking who performed the actions
keyPoints: 4720 = account created, 4728 = added to a global security group, 4672 = admin-privilege logon
The sequence together, not any single event, is the red flag
Also know 4624 (successful logon) and 4625 (failed logon) as core IDs
Always correlate with who performed the action and whether it was authorized

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies all three event IDs
Explains why the sequence together is suspicious
Mentions checking authorization/correlating the actor

questions.title: Writing a Basic Suricata Rule
questions.prompt: Write a basic Suricata rule that fires an alert whenever inbound HTTP traffic contains a User-Agent string matching sqlmap's default signature. Explain each part of the rule.
questions.code:
-- Goal: alert on any HTTP traffic whose User-Agent string matches
-- sqlmap's default User-Agent, a strong indicator of an automated
-- SQL-injection scanning tool.
questions.modelAnswer: A rule's skeleton is `action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options)`. The rule would be: `alert http any any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"Possible sqlmap scan detected"; http.user_agent; content:"sqlmap"; nocase; sid:1000001; rev:1;)`. Breaking it down: `alert` is the action (log and notify, without blocking, unlike `drop`), `http` is the protocol, `any any -> $HOME_NET any` means any source on any port to the protected network on any port, `http.user_agent` is a sticky buffer that scopes the following `content` match specifically to the User-Agent header rather than the whole payload, `nocase` makes the match case-insensitive, and `sid`/`rev` are the rule's required unique identifier and revision number.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as an alert, not a drop, at least initially -- sqlmap's default User-Agent is a strong signal but not proof of malicious intent on its own, since it could also be a security team's own scanning or a researcher, so I'd want a human looking at the context before anything gets blocked automatically. The piece I'd be most careful about is the `http.user_agent` sticky buffer -- without it, `content:"sqlmap"` would search the entire HTTP payload, which is a much noisier and less precise match than scoping it to just the header where I actually expect to find it.
questions.example: alert http any any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"Possible sqlmap scan detected"; http.user_agent; content:"sqlmap"; nocase; sid:1000001; rev:1;)
commonMistakes: Forgetting the http.user_agent sticky buffer and matching content against the whole packet instead
Omitting nocase and missing case variants of the string
Forgetting sid is required and must be unique
Using alert when the intent is actually to block (drop), or vice versa
keyPoints: Rule skeleton: action/protocol/src/dst/options
http.user_agent sticky buffer scopes the match to that header
nocase makes a content match case-insensitive
sid/rev are required and sid must be unique
alert logs; drop blocks inline (IPS mode only)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Syntactically correct, working rule
Correctly explains each rule component
Notes the alert-vs-drop distinction or a tuning consideration

questions.title: Writing a Basic KQL Query Against SigninLogs
questions.prompt: Write a KQL query against the SigninLogs table that returns the last day's failed sign-ins, showing only the time, user, app, IP address, and result code, in that order.
questions.code:
-- Table: SigninLogs (Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs in Sentinel)
-- Columns include: TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName,
-- IPAddress, ResultType ("0" = success, non-zero = failure)
questions.modelAnswer: `SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where ResultType != "0" | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, ResultType`. `ago(1d)` computes a relative time boundary one day back. `where` filters rows, and since KQL pipe order is execution order, filtering before projecting is more efficient on a large table than selecting columns first. `project` both selects and orders the output columns in the exact sequence listed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the time filter first, since `ago(1d)` is the cheapest and most effective way to shrink a potentially enormous table before doing anything else with it. One detail I'd double check is that ResultType is a string field in this table, so I compare it to `"0"`, not the number `0` -- that's a mistake I've seen trip people up when they assume it's numeric just because it looks like one.
questions.example:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType != "0"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, ResultType
commonMistakes: Using take/limit instead of a proper time filter, which samples rows rather than scoping by time
Comparing ResultType to the number 0 instead of the string "0"
Projecting before filtering, doing unnecessary work on a large table
Forgetting KQL's case sensitivity when referencing column names
keyPoints: `where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)` scopes by time
ResultType is a string field, compare to "0" not 0
project both selects and orders columns
Filter before projecting for efficiency on large tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, runnable KQL syntax
Correct time-scoping with ago()
Correct column selection and order via project

questions.title: Spotting a Password-Spray Pattern with KQL summarize
questions.prompt: Write a KQL query that ranks users by their number of failed sign-ins in the last day, from most to least, as a first step toward spotting a password-spray attack.
questions.modelAnswer: `SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where ResultType != "0" | summarize FailedSignIns = count() by UserPrincipalName | sort by FailedSignIns desc`. `summarize ... by` groups rows per user, and `count()` computes the aggregate within each group -- directly analogous to SQL's GROUP BY plus COUNT(*), but expressed in KQL's pipe syntax. This is the classic first-pass password-spray/brute-force detection pattern: a normal user has at most a handful of failed logins, while a spray target has noticeably more within a short window.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always my starting query for a suspected spray, because it's cheap to run and immediately surfaces who's getting hammered. I'd usually follow it up with a second pass adding `dcount(IPAddress)` to the same summarize, because a real password-spray tends to come from many distinct source IPs hitting one or a few accounts, whereas a single confused user locking themselves out tends to come from one IP -- that distinction matters a lot for how urgently I'd treat the result.
questions.example:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType != "0"
| summarize FailedSignIns = count() by UserPrincipalName
| sort by FailedSignIns desc
commonMistakes: Forgetting "by UserPrincipalName" and getting one aggregate for the whole table instead of per-user
Not sorting the result, making it hard to scan for the worst offenders
Treating a high failure count alone as proof of compromise without checking whether any attempt succeeded
Not considering dcount(IPAddress) as a second useful dimension
keyPoints: summarize count() by <column> is KQL's equivalent of GROUP BY + COUNT
Sort descending by the aggregate to surface the worst offenders first
A high failure count alone is a starting signal, not proof
dcount() for distinct-value counts (like distinct source IPs) strengthens the signal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct summarize/count/by syntax
Correct descending sort for ranking
Explains why this pattern indicates password spray

questions.title: NTFS Permissions vs. Share Permissions: the Effective Result
questions.prompt: A folder has share permissions set to 'Change' and NTFS permissions set to 'Read & Execute' for the same user. When that user accesses the folder over the network, what is their effective permission, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The effective permission is Read & Execute -- the more restrictive of the two always applies. Windows evaluates both the share-level permission (which governs network access only) and the NTFS-level permission (which applies regardless of access method), and the actual result is whichever one is more restrictive. Here, Change at the share level would allow modifying files, but Read & Execute at the NTFS level doesn't permit writing -- so the effective access caps at Read & Execute.
questions.professionalAnswer: The habit I'd follow in practice is to keep share permissions loose (often Everyone/Full Control at the share level in a lot of real environments) and do the actual enforcement entirely at the NTFS level, since NTFS also governs local, non-network access to the same folder, which share permissions have no say over at all. But I'd never assume that just because NTFS is doing the 'real' work -- both are still evaluated together over the network, and the most restrictive one wins every time.
commonMistakes: Assuming the two permission sets are additive rather than 'most restrictive wins'
Forgetting share permissions only apply over the network, not to local access to the same folder
Setting overly permissive share permissions assuming NTFS alone matters, without realizing both are still evaluated together
Not checking both permission layers when troubleshooting an access-denied report
keyPoints: Effective network permission = the more restrictive of share and NTFS
Share permissions only govern network access
NTFS permissions apply to both local and network access
Common real pattern: loose share permissions, NTFS does the actual enforcement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the effective permission
Correctly explains the 'most restrictive wins' rule
Notes share permissions only apply over the network

questions.title: Verifying a GPO Actually Applied
questions.prompt: You've linked a new GPO to an OU to enforce a password-lockout policy. How would you verify, on an actual client machine, whether that GPO has applied -- and what's the difference between a GPO simply being linked and it actually taking effect?
questions.modelAnswer: A GPO has to be linked to a site, domain, or OU to be in scope at all, but linking alone doesn't guarantee it applies. GPOs follow LSDOU inheritance order (Local, Site, Domain, OU), and a setting can be overridden by a GPO processed later in that order, or blocked by Block Inheritance at a lower OU -- unless the higher GPO is marked Enforced, which always wins over Block Inheritance. To verify on an actual client, force an immediate refresh with `gpupdate /force`, then confirm what actually won with `gpresult /r`, which produces a Resultant Set of Policy report showing exactly which GPOs applied, which were filtered out, and why.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd never trust the Group Policy Management Console's link view alone to tell me a setting actually applied -- that view only tells me what's linked, not what won. `gpresult /r` on the real client is what actually answers the question, because it shows the resultant policy after all the inheritance and precedence rules have played out. If the setting still isn't showing up there, my first suspicion is Block Inheritance somewhere below where I linked it, unless I remembered to mark my GPO as Enforced.
commonMistakes: Assuming linking a GPO is the same as it taking effect
Forgetting a lower-OU Block Inheritance setting can silently prevent a higher GPO from applying unless it's Enforced
Thinking gpupdate /force by itself proves the setting won, rather than just triggering a refresh
Checking only the GPMC link view instead of gpresult /r on the actual client
keyPoints: Linking is not the same as applying
GPOs follow LSDOU inheritance order
Block Inheritance can be overridden by Enforced
gpupdate /force triggers a refresh; gpresult /r (RSoP) is the real verification tool

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the link-vs-apply distinction
Correctly describes LSDOU/Enforced/Block Inheritance interaction
Names the correct verification commands

questions.title: A 'New Location' Login: False Positive or Real Threat?
questions.prompt: A SIEM fires a 'sign-in from a new location' alert for a user account. As the Tier 1 analyst, what specific pieces of evidence would you check before deciding whether to close this as a false positive or escalate it, and what single additional finding would make you escalate immediately even if the location itself seems explainable?
questions.modelAnswer: Validate against the raw sign-in logs rather than trusting the alert's own label, and scope by checking what else that account touched around the same time. Check whether the new location is consistent with known travel or remote work, whether there's a second suspicious sign-in close in time from a very different location (impossible travel), and whether MFA was genuinely satisfied or bypassed through a legacy, non-MFA-capable protocol. Critically, check what happened after the sign-in -- a new mail-forwarding rule, unusual file-share access, or an OAuth app consent grant. A finding like a hidden mailbox-forwarding rule discovered after the sign-in would force escalation even if the location alone seemed explainable, because post-login account activity is a far stronger compromise signal than location mismatch by itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd never close this off the location alone. My real checklist is: does the timing make sense (is this person known to travel or work remotely), is there a second sign-in close in time from somewhere implausibly far away, and -- the part I care about most -- did anything happen after the login that a legitimate user wouldn't normally do. I've seen a case that looked completely explainable as conference travel turn out to be a genuine compromise the moment someone found a hidden forwarding rule quietly routing anything mentioning 'invoice' or 'wire' to an external address. That single finding changes everything, regardless of how reasonable the location looked.
commonMistakes: Closing the alert based on the location alone without checking what the account did after logging in
Trusting the alert's own label instead of pulling the raw underlying logs
Not checking whether MFA was genuinely satisfied versus bypassed through a legacy protocol
Treating 'explainable' and 'safe' as the same thing
keyPoints: Validate against raw logs, don't trust the alert label alone
Scope by checking what the account did after sign-in, not just the sign-in itself
Impossible travel is a strong signal on its own
Post-login indicators (forwarding rules, OAuth consent, unusual access) often matter more than location

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Lists concrete evidence to check before deciding
Correctly distinguishes a benign explanation from a real compromise
Identifies a specific finding that forces escalation regardless

questions.title: Tuning a Rule That Fires on a Backup Service Account Every Night
questions.prompt: Your correlation rule for '5 failed logons then 1 success within 10 minutes' fires every single night at 2 AM for the same backup service account, and every time it turns out to be legitimate. The analyst team is starting to ignore the alert entirely. How would you fix this without just deleting the rule?
questions.modelAnswer: This is alert fatigue, which is a genuine security risk rather than just an annoyance, because analysts who learn to tune out a noisy-but-legitimate alert will also tune out the one night it's real. The fix is a scoped exclusion -- suppress this specific account from this specific rule, not from detection entirely -- or a threshold/timing adjustment if the root cause is something benign and predictable, like a password rotation causing a brief authentication gap. Whichever fix is used, document why the exclusion exists and revisit it periodically, since an undocumented, never-reviewed exclusion becomes its own blind spot -- if that same account is ever actually compromised, it now has a standing free pass from the rule.
questions.professionalAnswer: Deleting the rule is the tempting shortcut but it throws away detection for every other account, not just this one. I'd scope an exclusion narrowly to this specific service account on this specific rule, write down exactly why (the nightly backup job's known authentication timing), and put a reminder to revisit that exclusion periodically -- because an exclusion nobody ever looks at again is exactly the kind of thing that quietly becomes a permanent blind spot years later.
commonMistakes: Deleting the rule entirely, losing detection for every other account
Making the exclusion so broad it accidentally whitelists a human user's account too
Adding the exception without documenting why it exists
Never revisiting the exclusion, letting it become a permanent, forgotten blind spot
keyPoints: Alert fatigue is a real security risk, not just noise
Fix via scoped exclusion or threshold adjustment, not deletion
Document the reason for any exclusion
Periodically re-review exclusions so they don't become permanent blind spots

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies alert fatigue as the real underlying risk
Proposes a specific, scoped fix rather than deleting the rule
Mentions documentation and periodic review of the exclusion

questions.title: True Positive, False Positive, or Benign True Positive?
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a true positive, a false positive, and a 'benign true positive' in alert triage, and give a realistic example of each.
questions.modelAnswer: A true positive is an alert that correctly fired on something real and malicious. A false positive means the detection logic itself was wrong, or the activity it claimed to see didn't actually happen that way. A benign true positive means the alert correctly detected a real event exactly as described, but that event turns out to be legitimate rather than malicious -- for example, an 'admin logged in from a new country' alert that's entirely accurate, because the admin really is traveling. The distinction matters because a benign true positive means the detection logic is working exactly as intended and shouldn't be 'fixed,' while a false positive means the rule's actual logic needs tuning.
questions.professionalAnswer: The one people mix up most is benign true positive versus false positive, and getting that wrong has a real cost: if I treat a benign true positive as a false positive and 'tune' the rule to stop catching that pattern, I've just broken a detection that was working correctly, because the next time that exact pattern happens it might not be an admin's real travel. I try to always ask, specifically, 'did the thing the alert describes actually happen' separately from 'was that thing malicious,' because those are two different questions with two different fixes.
commonMistakes: Treating a benign true positive as the same thing as a false positive and tuning away a working rule
Assuming every alert that turns out harmless is automatically a false positive
Not documenting which category an alert fell into, losing visibility into how the rule is actually performing
Closing a benign true positive without recording context, forcing the next analyst to re-investigate from scratch
keyPoints: True positive = real detection of a real threat
False positive = the detection logic itself is wrong
Benign true positive = accurate detection of a real but legitimate event
The distinction determines whether the rule needs tuning or not
Documenting the classification matters for future triage and metrics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all three categories
Gives a realistic example distinguishing them
Explains why the distinction affects what action to take on the rule

questions.title: Locked Out After an SSH Hardening Change
questions.prompt: You pushed `PasswordAuthentication no` to a fleet of Linux servers to force key-based SSH only. Afterward, several engineers report they can no longer log in at all -- including some who claim they were using key-based auth already. What's the likely sequence of mistakes here, and what's the safer rollout order you should have followed?
questions.modelAnswer: The likely mistakes: the change was pushed to the whole fleet before actually confirming every affected user's public key was deployed and working under key-based auth, `sshd -t` likely wasn't run to syntax-check the config before reloading, and no out-of-band access path (console access, a break-glass account) was kept available in case something was missed. The safer order: actively verify key-based auth works for every user who needs it before disabling password auth at all -- don't just trust a claim that it's already set up -- always run `sshd -t` before reloading sshd, roll out to a pilot group first instead of the whole fleet, and keep a fallback access path available during the change.
questions.professionalAnswer: The phrase 'I was already using key-based auth' is exactly the claim I wouldn't take at face value before a change like this -- I'd actually test it myself for each affected user, because 'I think it's set up' and 'it's actually working right now' are two different things. I'd also never push a change like this to the whole fleet at once; a pilot group first would have surfaced this problem on a handful of machines instead of locking out the whole engineering team. And `sshd -t` before any reload is non-negotiable for me on an auth-related change specifically, because the failure mode here isn't a crash, it's a silent, total lockout.
commonMistakes: Pushing the change to the whole fleet at once instead of a pilot group first
Assuming users who claim they have key-based auth actually have a working, deployed key
Skipping sshd -t before reloading sshd
Not keeping any out-of-band access path available during the change
keyPoints: Verify key-based auth actually works for every affected user before disabling password auth
Always run sshd -t before reloading
Roll out to a pilot group first, not the whole fleet
Keep an out-of-band/break-glass access path available during any auth-hardening change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the likely root-cause mistakes
Proposes the correct, safer rollout order
Mentions keeping a fallback/out-of-band access path

questions.title: Diagnosing a Phishing-to-PowerShell LOLBin Chain
questions.prompt: Endpoint telemetry shows a user opened a Word document from an email attachment, and seconds later `winword.exe` spawned `powershell.exe` with an encoded command, which then made an outbound network connection to an unfamiliar IP. Why does this process chain alone -- even with no obvious malware file on disk -- already strongly indicate compromise, and what's the specific technique category this represents?
questions.modelAnswer: Word never legitimately needs to spawn PowerShell as a child process during normal use -- that parent-child relationship is itself the anomaly, regardless of what the PowerShell command actually does. This is a 'living off the land' (LOLBin) technique, where the attacker abuses a legitimate, signed system tool like PowerShell, usually reached through a malicious document macro, instead of dropping a custom malware binary, specifically to evade signature-based antivirus, which has nothing unusual to flag since PowerShell itself isn't malware. The `-EncodedCommand` flag is a known evasion technique used to obfuscate the actual payload from casual log review. EDR's process-tree visibility -- not signature-based antivirus -- is what catches this pattern, because it's watching parent-child relationships and command-line arguments, not file hashes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't wait for a malware file to show up before treating this as real. The process chain itself is the evidence -- Word spawning PowerShell is not something that happens in legitimate, everyday use, full stop. This is exactly the kind of thing signature antivirus is built to miss, because there's no malicious file to hash and flag; the 'malware' here is really just a built-in, trusted Windows tool being told to do something it was never supposed to do. The encoded command is a second red flag on top of the process-chain anomaly, since it's a known way attackers obscure what the command is actually doing from anyone glancing at the log.
commonMistakes: Waiting for a malicious file to appear on disk before treating the process chain itself as evidence
Not recognizing winword.exe spawning powershell.exe as an inherently abnormal parent-child relationship
Assuming signature-based antivirus would have caught this
Not flagging -EncodedCommand as a specific obfuscation indicator worth investigating on its own
keyPoints: LOLBins = abusing legitimate signed tools instead of custom malware to evade signature AV
The parent-child process relationship (Word spawning PowerShell) is itself the red flag
-EncodedCommand is a known obfuscation indicator
EDR's process-tree/command-line visibility, not file-hash AV, catches this pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as a LOLBin technique
Explains why the process-chain relationship alone is the red flag
Explains why signature AV would miss it but EDR catches it

questions.title: Windows Firewall Blocking Legitimate Traffic on the Wrong Profile
questions.prompt: A laptop can reach internal file shares fine on the office Wi-Fi, but when the same user connects from a coffee shop, the same connection attempt is silently blocked by Windows Firewall -- with no explicit rule blocking it. What's the most likely explanation, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: Windows Firewall maintains three independent profiles -- Domain, Private, and Public -- each with its own default posture and its own active rule set. The office network is likely classified as Domain or Private, where a custom inbound rule permitting the file-share traffic applies, while the coffee-shop Wi-Fi is classified as Public, where the default posture is far more restrictive and the custom rule either isn't scoped to that profile at all or was never configured for it. Confirm by checking the active network profile at each location (via Windows Security, or `Get-NetConnectionProfile` in PowerShell) and checking which profile(s) the relevant inbound rule is actually scoped to in Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to look for an explicit block rule, because there probably isn't one -- the real question is which profile Windows assigned to that coffee-shop network and whether the rule that works fine at the office was ever scoped to also apply there. `Get-NetConnectionProfile` tells me immediately what profile Windows picked, and then I'd go check the specific rule's profile scope in Advanced Security rather than assuming the rule set is identical everywhere.
commonMistakes: Assuming there must be an explicit block rule rather than realizing the rule simply isn't scoped to the Public profile
Not checking which network profile Windows actually assigned to the coffee-shop connection
Forgetting each profile has entirely independent rule sets and defaults, not one shared set with per-network overrides
Troubleshooting the file-share service itself before checking the firewall profile
keyPoints: Windows Firewall has three independent profiles (Domain/Private/Public) with separate defaults and rules
A rule can be fully present but simply not scoped to the active profile
Check the active profile with Get-NetConnectionProfile
Public profile defaults are deliberately more restrictive since the network isn't trusted

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the firewall-profile explanation
Proposes a concrete way to confirm it
Explains why profiles have different default postures

questions.title: One-Way Traffic Breaks After a Firewall Swap
questions.prompt: After replacing an old stateless packet-filtering firewall with a modern stateful one, a team reports that outbound web browsing from internal users completely stopped working, even though the new firewall's rule set looks like a faithful copy of the old one. What did the migration most likely miss?
questions.modelAnswer: A stateless firewall evaluates every packet independently against static rules, so the old rule set almost certainly needed an explicit inbound-allow rule just to permit return traffic, since nothing about connection state is assumed. A stateful firewall instead tracks a table of open connections and automatically permits matching reply traffic for a connection it already allowed outbound -- it doesn't need, and shouldn't rely on, a separate static inbound rule for replies. If the rule set was copied literally without re-thinking it for the new architecture, the most likely root cause is that the actual outbound-permit rule needed to initiate a brand-new connection was never explicitly carried over or correctly scoped, because the old design's reliance on paired static rules masked that the real outbound-allow was missing or mis-scoped in the copy.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trap here is treating 'faithful copy of the rule set' as proof the migration was done correctly, when a stateless and a stateful firewall simply don't behave the same way given the same rules. I'd check first whether a brand-new outbound connection -- not an existing one that was already open before the swap -- actually succeeds, because that's the real test. My bet is the outbound-permit rule itself either didn't make the jump cleanly or isn't scoped the way the new firewall expects, since the old setup's extra inbound-allow rule (needed only because it was stateless) was never really the thing doing the real work.
commonMistakes: Assuming a 'faithful copy' of a stateless rule set behaves identically once applied to a stateful firewall
Testing only existing, already-open connections instead of a brand-new connection after the migration
Not recognizing that stateful firewalls replace the need for a matching inbound-allow rule with automatic state-table tracking
Not re-verifying the actual outbound-permit rule exists and matches the new firewall's syntax and zones
keyPoints: Stateless firewalls need explicit rules for both directions of traffic
Stateful firewalls track connection state and auto-permit matching replies for an already-allowed outbound connection
A literal rule-set copy between the two architectures can silently drop the explicit outbound-allow rule the stateful firewall actually needs
Always test a brand-new connection, not just existing ones, after a firewall migration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the stateful-vs-stateless behavior difference
Identifies a plausible concrete root cause for the outage
Proposes a way to verify or test after the fix

questions.title: A GPO Setting Isn't Applying to One OU
questions.prompt: A password-complexity GPO applies correctly to every OU in the domain except one -- the Finance OU, where the old, weaker setting is still in effect. The GPO is definitely linked at the domain level. What are the two most likely explanations, and how would you tell which one it is?
questions.modelAnswer: The two most likely explanations: the Finance OU has Block Inheritance enabled, preventing the domain-level GPO from flowing down to it, or a separate, more specific GPO is linked directly to the Finance OU with a conflicting setting -- and because GPOs process in LSDOU order (Local, Site, Domain, OU), the OU-linked GPO processes last and wins unless the domain-level GPO is explicitly marked Enforced. Tell which one it is by running `gpresult /r` on a Finance machine, which reports exactly which GPOs applied, which were filtered out, and why -- including whether Block Inheritance or a precedence conflict is the actual cause -- rather than guessing from the GPMC console alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to diagnose this from the Group Policy Management Console's link view, because that only shows me what's linked, not what's actually winning on a real machine. `gpresult /r` on a Finance workstation tells me directly whether it's Block Inheritance cutting the domain GPO off, or a more specific Finance-OU GPO that's simply processing later and winning. If it turns out to be the latter, marking the domain-level GPO as Enforced would override that conflict outright.
commonMistakes: Assuming a domain-linked GPO is guaranteed to reach every OU regardless of local settings
Not checking for Block Inheritance as a distinct possibility from a conflicting local GPO
Trying to diagnose this purely from the GPMC link view instead of running gpresult /r on an affected machine
Forgetting that Enforced on the domain-level GPO overrides both Block Inheritance and a conflicting OU-level GPO
keyPoints: Two likely causes: Block Inheritance on the Finance OU, or a more specific conflicting GPO winning under LSDOU order
Enforced on the higher-level GPO overrides both
gpresult /r (RSoP) is the correct diagnostic tool, not just the GPMC link view

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both plausible causes
Correctly explains LSDOU order and Enforced's effect
Names the correct diagnostic command

questions.title: A Login Field Throws a Database Error After a Single Quote
questions.prompt: A tester types a single quote character into a login form's username field and the application responds with a raw database error message instead of 'invalid username.' What does this tell you is happening under the hood, and what's the real fix -- not just hiding the error message?
questions.modelAnswer: The single quote is breaking out of the intended string literal in a SQL query that's being built by directly concatenating user input into the query text -- the application is vulnerable to SQL injection, since unsanitized input is altering the query's actual structure, not just its data, which is exactly how an attacker could go on to bypass login authentication entirely or extract data. Hiding the error message only hides the symptom (information disclosure) and does nothing about the underlying vulnerability. The real fix is parameterized queries (prepared statements), where user input is always treated strictly as data and can never be interpreted as query syntax regardless of what characters it contains, backed up by input validation and output encoding as additional layers -- consistent with OWASP Top 10 guidance on injection.
questions.professionalAnswer: A raw database error coming back from a single quote is a gift to whoever's testing, honestly -- it's telling me the query is being built by string concatenation, and it's also a gift to an attacker, since that error message itself can leak database type and schema details. I'd point out immediately that just suppressing the error display doesn't fix anything underneath -- the actual fix is switching to parameterized queries, where the database treats whatever I typed as pure data no matter what characters are in it, not a blocklist of 'dangerous' characters, which is always going to be incomplete.
commonMistakes: Treating this as just an 'ugly error message' problem and fixing only error display or logging
Trying to sanitize input with a blocklist of dangerous characters instead of switching to parameterized queries
Not recognizing a raw database error is itself a reconnaissance gift to an attacker
Assuming this only matters for login forms and not any other field that reaches a database query
keyPoints: A raw DB error after a single quote is a concrete SQL injection indicator, not a cosmetic bug
The input is altering query structure/logic, not just its data
The real fix is parameterized queries/prepared statements
This maps directly to OWASP Top 10's injection category

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses SQL injection as the underlying issue
Explains why hiding the error message doesn't fix anything
Proposes parameterized queries as the real fix

questions.title: An 'Impossible Travel' Alert Turns Into Four Related Events
questions.prompt: An 'impossible travel' sign-in alert comes in for one user account. When you pull together everything else tied to that account in the same timeframe, you find a new mailbox-forwarding rule, an OAuth app consent grant, and a finance-folder download -- none of which triggered their own alert. What does this tell you about scoping an incident, and why can't Tier 1 rely on individual alerts alone to catch this?
questions.modelAnswer: Scoping means deliberately pulling together everything else tied to the same entities -- the account, the device, the IP -- in the relevant timeframe, rather than treating the triggering alert as the whole story. Each follow-on action individually might look unremarkable or fall below any single rule's threshold, since a mailbox rule change, an OAuth consent, and a file download are all things legitimate users do constantly -- that's exactly why no detection rule fired on any of them alone. It's only once they're pulled together around the same compromised account, in the same tight window, that the pattern becomes obviously malicious. This is why incident-scale triage, grouping by shared entities, catches what single-alert-at-a-time triage misses, and why closing a ticket the moment the original alert looks 'resolved' can leave a fuller compromise still in progress.
questions.professionalAnswer: None of those three follow-on actions would have raised my eyebrows on their own -- that's the point. A mailbox rule change happens all the time, an OAuth consent happens all the time, a file download happens all the time. It's only when I actively pull everything tied to that specific account in that specific window that the combination stops looking like noise and starts looking like a clear compromise chain. That's exactly why I don't consider a ticket closed just because the triggering alert's specific scenario is explained -- I go look at what else that account did around the same time, every time.
commonMistakes: Treating the original alert as the entire incident instead of actively pulling related activity for the same entities
Assuming 'no alert fired' on the forwarding rule or OAuth consent means nothing suspicious happened
Closing the ticket once the triggering alert's specific condition is explained, without checking what else happened around it
Not recognizing attackers often chain several individually-quiet actions to stay under each rule's threshold
keyPoints: Scoping = actively pulling together everything tied to the same entities in the same timeframe
Individually quiet actions can combine into an obvious compromise once correlated
Attackers often deliberately stay under each rule's individual threshold
Tier 1 triage that stops at the original alert can miss the fuller picture

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what scoping means in this context
Explains why none of the follow-on actions triggered their own alert
Explains the risk of relying on single-alert triage alone

questions.title: Defense in Depth: Five Layers
questions.prompt: What are the five layers in a typical defense-in-depth model, and walk through how a single phishing email click would be expected to pass through -- or get stopped by -- each layer.
questions.modelAnswer: The five layers, outside-in, are Perimeter, Network, Endpoint, Access control, and Monitoring/logging. Walking a phishing click through them: Perimeter -- an email/web gateway might catch and block the malicious link before delivery. Network -- if it lands anyway, network segmentation and firewall rules limit what the resulting connection can actually reach. Endpoint -- EDR or antivirus on the clicked machine might catch the payload executing. Access control -- even if the endpoint is compromised, least-privilege access and MFA limit what the attacker's resulting session can actually do. Monitoring/logging -- even if every prior layer fails silently, logging and SIEM correlation is what eventually surfaces the activity for a human to respond to. The point isn't stacking more tools; it's that each layer's failure is independent, so one layer being bypassed doesn't automatically mean the next one fails too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always walk this through with one concrete scenario rather than just listing the layers, because the real value of the model only shows up when you trace an actual click through it. If the gateway misses the phishing email, that doesn't mean the attack succeeds -- it just means the next layer, network segmentation, is now the thing standing between a compromised endpoint and anything valuable. If that fails too, EDR on the endpoint is the next shot. The layers are deliberately different kinds of control, not five copies of the same tool, which is exactly why one bypass doesn't cascade into all of them failing together.
commonMistakes: Listing the layers without walking the phishing example through each one concretely
Assuming defense in depth just means 'buy more security tools' rather than genuinely independent failure modes
Forgetting access control and monitoring/logging count as real layers, not just perimeter/network/endpoint
Treating the layers as redundant copies of the same control type rather than genuinely different kinds of protection
keyPoints: Five layers: Perimeter, Network, Endpoint, Access control, Monitoring/logging
Each layer should fail independently of the others
The model's value is genuinely different control types, not duplicated tools
Walking one real scenario through every layer demonstrates understanding

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly lists all five layers
Walks the phishing example through each layer accurately
Explains the independent-failure principle
